messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Graphic Designer
- Trauma Type: Police
- Pcl5: 40

He describes the light first. Not the red and blue of the squad car, but the fluorescent white of the interrogation room. A flat, buzzing glare that erased every shadow. He remembers thinking it sounded exactly like a dying hard drive — a high-pitched whine every graphic designer knows. In his world, light is something he manipulates with precision: exposure, temperature, shadow depth. In that room, there was no subtlety. Just a harsh, unforgiving brightness that made him feel exposed down to his bones.

The incident happened six months ago. A Tuesday night. He had been at a client meeting, finalizing a branding deck for a tech startup. He remembers feeling pleased with his work, the kind of quiet satisfaction that comes from a perfectly balanced layout. The drive home was routine. Then the lights appeared behind him. Two patrol cars. He pulled over immediately, hands on the steering wheel at ten and two. He thought it was a mistake. It was a mistake — but not the kind that gets corrected quickly.

They told him he matched the description of a suspect. Someone had used a license plate similar to his in an armed robbery. He was pulled from his car, searched, and handcuffed on the curb in full view of passing traffic. He kept his voice calm, professional, cooperative. He asked, "Can you tell me what this is about?" No one answered directly. They took him to the station. He spent fourteen hours in a holding cell, the fluorescent light humming its broken-drive song, the air thick with disinfectant and the distant shouts of other men. He was released at dawn without an explanation or an apology. "You're free to go."

He has not felt free since.

At the studio, he moved his entire desk so his back is against the wall and he faces the door. He cannot concentrate. He used to lose himself in kerning, in the quiet logic of visual hierarchy. Now his mind snags on every sound — the creak of the office door, a raised voice in the hallway, the hum of his computer fan. That hum is the worst. It pulls him back into the cell. He recently abandoned a project halfway through because the client's brand colors included a deep navy blue. He told his boss the palette felt "off." The truth was simpler and more shameful: the blue was the exact shade of the patrol car's interior. He couldn't look at it.

At home, his wife Anika says he is a ghost. He doesn't laugh at her jokes. When she touches his shoulder, he flinches before he can stop himself. He spends his evenings on the couch, scrolling through his phone without seeing anything, listening to the street. Every car door is a potential threat. Every distant siren makes his chest seize. He has stopped driving on the street where he was pulled over. He takes a fifteen-minute detour instead. He avoids police stations, squad cars, even security guards. A glimpse of a uniform in a grocery store parking lot sends his heart racing.

He replays the arrest constantly. He asks himself what he could have done differently. He was polite, compliant, willing. It didn't matter. He has carried this heavy, invisible weight ever since. Anika told him last week she felt like she was losing him. That is why he is here. He sits on the edge of the chair, back straight, hands clasped, eyes flicking to the door. He is a man who once believed the world followed the same rules as good design — balanced, intentional, fair. That belief is gone now. He is still searching for something to replace it.
